claim: Cell size is controlled to be within a specific range to support physiological function.
source: Cell size is controlled to be within a specific range to support physiological function.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell size control supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: Cells use diverse mechanisms ranging from 'sizers' to 'adders' to control their size.
source: To control their size, cells use diverse mechanisms ranging from 'sizers', in which differences in cell size are compensated for in a single cell division cycle, to 'adders', in which a constant amount of cell growth occurs in each cell cycle.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to known cell size control mechanisms in the literature.

claim: In sizers, differences in cell size are compensated for in a single cell division cycle.
source: To control their size, cells use diverse mechanisms ranging from 'sizers', in which differences in cell size are compensated for in a single cell division cycle, to 'adders', in which a constant amount of cell growth occurs in each cell cycle.
evidence: This is a definition of sizer mechanisms based on established terminology.

claim: In adders, a constant amount of cell growth occurs in each cell cycle.
source: To control their size, cells use diverse mechanisms ranging from 'sizers', in which differences in cell size are compensated for in a single cell division cycle, to 'adders', in which a constant amount of cell growth occurs in each cell cycle.
evidence: This is a definition of adder mechanisms based on established terminology.

claim: If the mechanism is based on a G1 size control and an S/G2/M timer, as found for budding yeast and some human cells, adders likely evolve.
source: If the mechanism is based on a G1 size control and an S/G2/M timer, as found for budding yeast and some human cells, adders likely evolve.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary simulations performed in this study.

claim: If the G1 phase is significantly longer than the S/G2/M phase, as is often the case in mammalian cells in vivo, sizers become more likely.
source: But, if the G1 phase is significantly longer than the S/G2/M phase, as is often the case in mammalian cells in vivo, sizers become more likely.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary simulations and observations about mammalian cells.

claim: Sizers evolve when the cell cycle structure is inverted so that G1 is a timer, while S/G2/M performs size control, as is the case for the fission yeast S. pombe.
source: Sizers also evolve when the cell cycle structure is inverted so that G1 is a timer, while S/G2/M performs size control, as is the case for the fission yeast S. pombe.
evidence: This claim is supported by evolutionary simulations mimicking S. pombe cell cycle structure.

claim: For some size control networks, cell size consistently decreases in each cycle until a burst of cell cycle inhibitor drives an extended G1 phase much like the cell division cycle of the green algae Chlamydomonas.
source: For some size control networks, cell size consistently decreases in each cycle until a burst of cell cycle inhibitor drives an extended G1 phase much like the cell division cycle of the green algae Chlamydomonas.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolved networks showing this behavior in simulations.

claim: These size control networks evolved self-organized criticality.
source: That these size control networks evolved such self-organized criticality shows how the evolution of complex systems can drive the emergence of critical processes.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the evolved networks showing power-law distributions and critical behavior.

claim: Cell size sets the scale of subcellular compartments, cellular biosynthetic capacity, metabolism, mechanical properties, surface-to-volume ratios, and molecular transport.
source: Cell size is fundamental to cell physiology and function because it sets the scale of subcellular compartments, cellular biosynthetic capacity, metabolism, mechanical properties, surface-to-volume ratios, and molecular transport (Chan and Marshall, 2010; Ginzberg et al., 2015; Neurohr et al., 2019; Zatulovskiy and Skotheim, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Cells within a particular type are generally uniform in size.
source: While different types of cells vary enormously in size to perform their functions, cells within a particular type are generally uniform in size indicating that cell growth may be accurately coupled to division and differentiation processes.
evidence: This is based on general observations in cell biology.

claim: Cell growth is accurately coupled to division and differentiation processes.
source: While different types of cells vary enormously in size to perform their functions, cells within a particular type are generally uniform in size indicating that cell growth may be accurately coupled to division and differentiation processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells within a type are uniform in size.

claim: The molecules controlling cell division vary across the tree of life with the most striking differences separating eukaryotes and bacteria.
source: On a phenomenological level, there are many commonalities in how cells regulate their size even though the molecules controlling cell division vary across the tree of life with the most striking differences separating eukaryotes and bacteria.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of molecular differences across domains of life.

claim: A 'sizer' has a slope of –1 so that all variation in cell mass at birth is compensated for in one cell cycle.
source: A 'sizer' has a slope of –1 so that all variation in cell mass at birth is compensated for in one cell cycle, whereas an 'adder' has a slope of 0 so that each cell adds the same amount of mass during the cell cycle regardless of initial size.
evidence: This is a definition based on quantitative characterization of size control.

claim: An 'adder' has a slope of 0 so that each cell adds the same amount of mass during the cell cycle regardless of initial size.
source: A 'sizer' has a slope of –1 so that all variation in cell mass at birth is compensated for in one cell cycle, whereas an 'adder' has a slope of 0 so that each cell adds the same amount of mass during the cell cycle regardless of initial size.
evidence: This is a definition based on quantitative characterization of size control.

claim: In the case of an adder, control is weaker so that multiple cell cycles are required for a particularly large or small cell to return to the average cell size.
source: In the case of an adder, control is weaker so that multiple cell cycles are required for a particularly large or small cell to return to the average cell size.
evidence: This is inferred from the definition and mathematical properties of adders.

claim: Fission yeast and mouse epidermal stem cells exhibit 'sizers'.
source: Fission yeast and mouse epidermal stem cells exhibit 'sizers', and most bacteria, archaea, and cultured human cell lines exhibit behavior closer to adders (Cadart et al., 2018; Eun et al., 2018; Jun et al., 2018; Sveiczer et al., 1996; Westfall and Levin, 2017; Willis and Huang, 2017; Xie and Skotheim, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Most bacteria, archaea, and cultured human cell lines exhibit behavior closer to adders.
source: Fission yeast and mouse epidermal stem cells exhibit 'sizers', and most bacteria, archaea, and cultured human cell lines exhibit behavior closer to adders (Cadart et al., 2018; Eun et al., 2018; Jun et al., 2018; Sveiczer et al., 1996; Westfall and Levin, 2017; Willis and Huang, 2017; Xie and Skotheim, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Adders have been observed more often than sizers.
source: Thus, while diverse size control behaviors have been observed, adders have been observed more often than sizers.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited experimental observations.

claim: Evolutionary algorithms are a class of machine learning techniques aiming at mimicking evolutionary processes.
source: Evolutionary algorithms are a class of machine learning techniques aiming at mimicking evolutionary processes (Crombach, 2021; François, 2014; François and Hakim, 2004; Xiong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Solutions found by evolutionary algorithms are constrained by their evolutionary paths followed and present similar characteristics to biologically evolved systems.
source: Furthermore, solutions found by evolutionary algorithms are constrained by their evolutionary paths followed and present similar characteristics to biologically evolved systems (Schaerli et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cell size is regulated through the cell cycle control network that governs transitions from one phase of the cell cycle to the next.
source: Cell size is regulated through the cell cycle control network that governs transitions from one phase of the cell cycle to the next.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of cell cycle regulation.

claim: The division cycle can be broken up into distinct phases that are characterized by different molecular activities.
source: The division cycle can be broken up into distinct phases that are characterized by different molecular activities (Morgan, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a cell cycle textbook.

claim: Size control in general has been associated with either the G1/S transition or mitosis at the end of the cell cycle.
source: This is because size control in general has been associated with either the G1/S transition or mitosis at the end of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from cell cycle studies.

claim: Simulations in which size control takes place in G1 phase converge toward an adder mechanism for the entire cell cycle.
source: Simulations in which size control takes place in G1 phase converge toward an adder mechanism for the entire cell cycle and identified an active quantity sensing mechanism similar to dilution-based mechanisms previously identified experimentally (Chen et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2019; Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented in the study.

claim: The evolved networks identified an active quantity sensing mechanism similar to dilution-based mechanisms previously identified experimentally.
source: Simulations in which size control takes place in G1 phase converge toward an adder mechanism for the entire cell cycle and identified an active quantity sensing mechanism similar to dilution-based mechanisms previously identified experimentally (Chen et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2019; Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data and citations to experimental work.

claim: A relatively shorter S/G2/M phase favors sizer mechanisms.
source: A relatively shorter S/G2/M phase favors sizer mechanisms, while longer S/G2/M phases favor adders.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results.

claim: Longer S/G2/M phases favor adders.
source: A relatively shorter S/G2/M phase favors sizer mechanisms, while longer S/G2/M phases favor adders.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results.

claim: Inverting the model so that cell size controls S/G2/M and G1 is a timer, like in fission yeast, results in more sizer-like control.
source: Moreover, inverting the model so that cell size controls S/G2/M and G1 is a timer, like in fission yeast, results in more sizer-like control.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results.

claim: Adders arise when cell size is controlled at a point intermediate in the cell cycle, like the G1/S transition.
source: Thus, we anticipate adders arise when cell size is controlled at a point intermediate in the cell cycle, like the G1/S transition, while sizers will appear when cell size regulates a point later in the cell cycle, as is the case when G1 is proportionally longer, or control takes place at the transition to mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Sizers will appear when cell size regulates a point later in the cell cycle, as is the case when G1 is proportionally longer, or control takes place at the transition to mitosis.
source: Thus, we anticipate adders arise when cell size is controlled at a point intermediate in the cell cycle, like the G1/S transition, while sizers will appear when cell size regulates a point later in the cell cycle, as is the case when G1 is proportionally longer, or control takes place at the transition to mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: The evolved network implements a simplified relaxation oscillator.
source: Schematic of our seed network topology implementing a simplified relaxation oscillator.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: Cell cycle state is encoded via a binary switch called 'S/G2/M Switch' that is 0 in G1 and 1 in S/G2/M.
source: Cell cycle state (G1 or S/G2/M) is encoded via a binary switch called 'S/G2/M Switch' that is 0 in G1 and 1 in S/G2/M.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: S/G2/M is modeled as a pure timer of fixed duration with some uniform noise.
source: After progressing through G1/S, cells enter S/G2/M which we model as a pure timer of fixed duration with some uniform noise.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Cell volume grows exponentially and is divided symmetrically following mitosis.
source: Cell volume grows exponentially and is divided symmetrically following mitosis.
evidence: This is a description of the model assumptions.

claim: The initial quantity sensing oscillator does not perform size control and instead results in unstable growth where size deviations are amplified at each generation.
source: Thus, the network needs to evolve some other interactions and/or parameters to go beyond a simple G1 inhibitor driven by production in S/G2/M to create a viable cell lineage.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: At some point in evolution (around epoch 700 for this particular simulation), some weak control mechanism suddenly evolves, preventing cells from becoming too big without imposing a tight control on the average volume.
source: At some point in evolution (around epoch 700 for this particular simulation), some weak control mechanism suddenly evolves, preventing cells from becoming too big without imposing a tight control on the average volume (see also Figure 5 for an explicit example of how this is done).
evidence: This is observed in the evolutionary trajectory shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In budding yeast, the Whi5 protein is passively diluted in G1 to increase the stochastic rate of progression through the G1/S transition.
source: In budding yeast, the Whi5 protein is passively diluted in G1 to increase the stochastic rate of progression through the G1/S transition.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of budding yeast cell cycle control.

claim: An active titration mechanism is required to obtain G1 size control in the evolved network setup.
source: This is precisely why an active titration mechanism is required to obtain G1 size control in our setup.
evidence: This is inferred from the model mechanism.

claim: Model A2 exhibits overall a weak adder behavior similar to that found in Model A1.
source: If we perturb cell size to examine the dynamics of the return to steady state and look at the added volume during the cell cycle, we again see overall a weak adder behavior similar to that found in Model A1 (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: This is shown in simulation data in Figure 2I-J.

claim: Model A2 behaves as a sizer for volumes smaller than the equilibrium volume.
source: In contrast, Model A2 behaves as a sizer for volumes smaller than the equilibrium volume.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At higher volumes Model A2 behaves more like an adder/timer similar to Model A1.
source: However, at higher volumes it behaves more like an adder/timer similar to Model A1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Similar behavior was observed experimentally in budding yeast.
source: Similar behavior was observed experimentally in budding yeast (Chandler-Brown et al., 2017; Delarue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Both Models A1 and A2 approximate an adder near the equilibrium size, but their behavior differs further from equilibrium where for smaller volumes, Model A1 is still an adder while Model A2 is a sizer.
source: Thus, both Models A1 and A2 approximate an adder near the equilibrium size, but their behavior differs further from equilibrium where for smaller volumes, Model A1 is still an adder while Model A2 is a sizer.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The evolutionary algorithm selects networks that implement adders rather than sizers near the equilibrium size.
source: So far, our evolutionary algorithm selects networks that implement adders rather than sizers near the equilibrium size.
evidence: This is observed across multiple evolutionary simulations.

claim: This is surprising because sizers are in principle better than adders at controlling cell size and reducing the CV of the size distribution at birth.
source: This is surprising because sizers are in principle better than adders at controlling cell size and reducing the CV of the size distribution at birth, which is one of our fitness functions.
evidence: This is based on the theoretical properties of sizers versus adders.

claim: The best studied, and highly accurate sizer, is found in the fission yeast S. pombe.
source: The best studied, and highly accurate sizer, is found in the fission yeast S. pombe (Fantes, 1977; Sveiczer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: In contrast to budding yeast and human cells, where the size control takes place largely in G1 phase, fission yeast exerts size control later in the cell cycle at the G2/M transition.
source: In contrast to budding yeast and human cells, where the size control takes place largely in G1 phase, fission yeast exerts size control later in the cell cycle at the G2/M transition.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cell cycle control in different organisms.

claim: When the cell cycle structure is inverted so that G1 is a timer and S/G2/M is a sizer like in S. pombe, more sizer-like networks evolve than in the control experiment.
source: When the cell cycle structure is inverted so that G1 is a timer and S/G2/M is a sizer like it is in the fission yeast S. pombe, we found that more sizer-like networks evolve than in the control experiment (Figure 4B, Welch's t-test on agglomerated data p=0.03).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: Having a network structure like the fission yeast S. pombe promotes sizers, while having the size control portion of the cell cycle earlier, as in the budding yeast S. cerevisiae, promotes adders.
source: This shows that having a network structure like the fission yeast S. pombe promotes sizers, while having the size control portion of the cell cycle earlier, as in the budding yeast S. cerevisiae, promotes adders.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results comparing different cell cycle structures.

claim: Performing simulations using cell cycle network structures of budding and fission yeast results in the evolution of size control mechanisms that reflect those that are naturally occurring.
source: Thus, performing simulations using cell cycle network structures of these two yeasts results in the evolution of size control mechanisms that reflect those that are naturally occurring.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of simulation results with experimental observations.

claim: A recent study examining mouse epidermal stem cells growing and dividing in the skin found both a strong sizer and that this sizer was largely due to the size-dependent regulation of G1.
source: However, a recent study examining mouse epidermal stem cells growing and dividing in the skin found both a strong sizer and that this sizer was largely due to the size-dependent regulation of G1 (Mesa et al., 2018; Xie and Skotheim, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The S/G2/M phase of the cell cycle is similar in duration in cultured cells and the epidermal stem cells in vivo at ~12 hr.
source: While the S/G2/M phase of the cell cycle is similar in duration in cultured cells and the epidermal stem cells in vivo at ~12 hr, the G1 phase extends ~fivefold from ~10 hr in culture to ~50 hr in vivo (Cadart et al., 2018; Xie and Skotheim, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The G1 phase extends ~fivefold from ~10 hr in culture to ~50 hr in vivo.
source: While the S/G2/M phase of the cell cycle is similar in duration in cultured cells and the epidermal stem cells in vivo at ~12 hr, the G1 phase extends ~fivefold from ~10 hr in culture to ~50 hr in vivo (Cadart et al., 2018; Xie and Skotheim, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The overall size control behavior can be dominated by the relatively longer cell cycle phase.
source: This suggests the hypothesis that the overall size control behavior can be dominated by the relatively longer cell cycle phase, as is likely the case for the G1 phase of epidermal stem cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observations about epidermal stem cells.

claim: When a timer in S/G2/M is relatively shorter compared to G1, more sizer-like behavior can evolve.
source: When a timer in S/G2/M is relatively shorter compared to G1, we generally see more sizer-like behavior can evolve (Figure 4C, Welch's t-test on agglomerated data p=4 x 10–3), while when it is relatively longer, we see more adder-like or even timer-like behavior (Figure 4D, Welch's t-test on agglomerated data p<10–4).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4C with statistical analysis.

claim: When the S/G2/M timer is relatively longer compared to G1, more adder-like or even timer-like behavior evolves.
source: When a timer in S/G2/M is relatively shorter compared to G1, we generally see more sizer-like behavior can evolve (Figure 4C, Welch's t-test on agglomerated data p=4 x 10–3), while when it is relatively longer, we see more adder-like or even timer-like behavior (Figure 4D, Welch's t-test on agglomerated data p<10–4).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation results in Figure 4D with statistical analysis.

claim: Increasing the noise in the timer progressively reduced the amount of size control done by the network.
source: Increasing the noise in the timer progressively reduced the amount of size control done by the network (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in simulation results in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: The fixed duration of S/G2/M allows the system to accurately reset protein concentrations for the subsequent cell cycle to promote accurate G1 control.
source: This is likely because the fixed duration of S/G2/M allows the system to accurately reset protein concentrations for the subsequent cell cycle to promote accurate G1 control (Willis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results and supported by a citation.

claim: The structural features of the cell cycle are important for determining what type of size control ultimately evolves.
source: Taken together, our simulations show how the structural features of the cell cycle are important for determining what type of size control ultimately evolves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: G1 control is more conducive to the evolution of adders, while S/G2/M control is more conducive to sizers.
source: G1 control is more conducive to the evolution of adders, while S/G2/M control is more conducive to sizers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Size control can be dominated by the cell cycle phase of longest duration.
source: Moreover, size control can be dominated by the cell cycle phase of longest duration and is modulated by the specific selection criteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: In the early stages of evolution, small cell size triggers an overshoot to a large cell size, which is then reduced through a series of rapid divisions.
source: In the early stages of the evolution (epoch 650), we typically see dynamics where small cell size triggers an overshoot to a large cell size, which is then reduced through a series of rapid divisions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the evolutionary trajectory in Figure 5A.

claim: Because of the small-size-triggered overshoot, the system behaves more like a sizer when the average behavior is analyzed.
source: Because of this small-size-triggered overshoot, the system behaves more like a sizer when the average behavior is analyzed (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The high degree of variability in the cell cycles leads to a broad distribution of volumes.
source: However, the high degree of variability in the cell cycles also leads to a broad distribution of volumes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The variability in volume is attenuated in later epochs where there are fewer and smaller volume overshoots triggered by small cell size.
source: The variability in volume is attenuated in later epochs where there are fewer and smaller volume overshoots triggered by small cell size (Figure 5D–I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D-I.

claim: A two-step evolutionary pathway exists: first, a strong but imprecise sizer mechanism evolves, then the variability is reduced by attenuating the strength of the size control response.
source: Taken together, these analyses suggest a two-step evolutionary pathway, consistent with the evolutionary dynamics first seen in Figure 2A. First, a strong but imprecise sizer mechanism evolves where, because of noise in the system, small variations in volume lead to a dramatic overcorrection and overshoot of the target volume. The variability in volume produced by this overshoot is then reduced by attenuating the strength of the size control response.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary trajectories shown in Figures 2A and 5.

claim: If some aspects of protein synthesis and degradation are subject to Poisson fluctuations, such fluctuations produce larger concentration fluctuations in smaller cells.
source: If some aspects of protein synthesis and degradation are subject to Poisson fluctuations, we expect such fluctuations to produce larger concentration fluctuations in smaller cells.
evidence: This is based on statistical principles of Poisson processes.

claim: If the cell could sense the size of concentration fluctuations, it would be able to harness the cell size-dependence of such stochastic fluctuations to regulate cell division and control cell size.
source: Thus, if the cell could sense the size of concentration fluctuations in some way, it would be able to harness the cell size-dependence of such stochastic fluctuations to regulate cell division and control cell size.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the size-dependence of molecular noise.

claim: The low volume regime occasionally leads to a considerable increase in G1 length and a correspondingly very large cell at division.
source: Thus, the low volume regime occasionally leads to a considerable increase in G1 length and a correspondingly very large cell at division.
evidence: This is observed in the dynamics of Model B shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The probability distribution of cell cycle durations follows a power law.
source: Interestingly, the probability distribution of cell cycle durations follows a power law (Figure 6F), which is due to the very broad distributions of G1 duration at lower cell volumes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F with a fitted scaling exponent.

claim: The evolved size control network exhibits self-organized criticality (SOC).
source: We conclude that our evolved size control network exhibits SOC based on several observations.
evidence: This is inferred from the power-law distributions and the feedback between order and control parameters.

claim: SOC is defined as a system where an order parameter feeds back on a control parameter.
source: SOC is defined as a system where an order parameter feeds back on a control parameter (Sornette et al., 1995; Vidiella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: Evolution tuned the system to be near a bifurcation.
source: Interestingly, evolution tuned the system to be near a bifurcation (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I and inferred from the dynamics.

claim: The last decade saw an explosion of time lapse microscopy studies measuring how cells control their size.
source: The last decade saw an explosion of time lapse microscopy studies measuring how cells control their size.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the citations throughout the paper.

claim: These studies revealed diverse phenomena that are characterized by the correlation between cell size at birth and cell size at division.
source: These studies revealed diverse phenomena that are characterized by the correlation between cell size at birth and cell size at division.
evidence: This is based on the literature cited throughout the paper.

claim: The evolved network implements an effective dilution of a cell cycle inhibitor that is conceptually similar to the well-described inhibitor dilution models of budding yeast, human cells, and Arabidopsis plants.
source: Thus, our evolved network implements an effective dilution of a cell cycle inhibitor that is conceptually similar to the well-described inhibitor dilution models of budding yeast, human cells, and Arabidopsis plants (D'Ario et al., 2021; Schmoller et al., 2015; Xie and Skotheim, 2020; Zatulovskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison drawn by the authors and supported by citations.

claim: Evolution simulations were not deterministic and there was no one-to-one correspondence between a given evolutionary pressure and any one specific cell size control mechanism.
source: First, it is worth noting that our evolution simulations were not deterministic. There was no one-to-one correspondence between a given evolutionary pressure and any one specific cell size control mechanism.
evidence: This is observed across the multiple evolutionary simulations performed.

claim: A low noise adder can produce a lower CV than a higher noise sizer.
source: It is therefore possible that a low noise adder can produce a lower CV than a higher noise sizer.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of size control mechanisms and noise.

claim: Sizers will always return the cell size to be within the steady state distribution within a cell cycle in response to large deviations.
source: However, we anticipate even noisy sizers will be better than adders at controlling cell size in response to large deviations away from the steady state distribution. This is because sizers will always return the cell size to be within the steady state distribution within a cell cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the definition and properties of sizers.

claim: A natural step in many simulated evolutions is a system with strong sizers at very small volume only.
source: They are also suggestive of evolutionary pathways: despite different evolutionary modalities and control types, a natural step in many of our simulated evolutions is a system with strong sizers at very small volume only (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is observed in the evolutionary trajectories shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Having size-dependent transitions later in the cell cycle selects for sizers, while having such transitions earlier selects for adders.
source: Taken together, these simulations suggest the principle that having size-dependent transitions later in the cell cycle selects for sizers, while having such transitions earlier selects for adders.
evidence: This is a principle inferred from the simulation results.

claim: This is the first example where self-organized criticality is obtained in artificially evolved models of gene networks performing a well-defined function.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first example where self-organized criticality is obtained in artificially evolved models of gene networks performing a well-defined function and is consistent with the idea that evolution of complex systems can favor the emergence of critical processes.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Volume is divided by 2 at each division after which one of the two daughter cells is followed.
source: Volume is divided by 2 at each division after which we follow one of the two daughter cells.
evidence: This is a description of the model assumptions.

claim: Upon passing the G1/S transition, cells are committed to division and there is a fixed time delay before they divide thus modeling S/G2/M as a timer.
source: Upon passing the G1/S transition, we assume cells are committed to division and there is a fixed time delay before they divide thus modeling S/G2/M as a timer (Chandler-Brown et al., 2017; Doncic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure supported by citations.

claim: The noise in the G1/S transition timing and S/G2/M timer duration creates natural cell to cell variability in volume that needs to be compensated for by the evolved mechanism.
source: This, along with the noise in S/G2/M timer duration, creates natural cell to cell variability in volume that needs to be compensated for by the evolved mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the model structure.

claim: This interaction systematically appears in the initial stages of evolution simulations when not included initially.
source: We initially ran simulations without this specific interaction but found that it systematically appears in the initial stages of evolution simulations. We therefore included it in the initial network to speed up our simulations.
evidence: This is observed in preliminary simulations.

claim: The dynamics of the simple cell-cycle model are similar to models of cell cycles based on relaxation oscillators.
source: Typical dynamics of this simple cell-cycle model are represented in Figure 1. These dynamics are similar to models of cell cycles based on relaxation oscillators (Cross, 2003; Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison supported by citations.
